extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science, philosophy, and logic interested in identifying and avoiding fallacies in argument and induction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for recognizing, classifying, and avoiding common logical fallacies (analogical, generalization, ratiocinative, and ambiguity-based) in scientific and philosophical argumentation. Emphasizes checking premises, meanings of terms, and causal connections when evaluating arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: False analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments from remote analogies or metaphors do not prove; the applicability of the metaphor is the very thing to be made out. "It has to be shown that in the two cases asserted to be analogous, the same law is really operating; that between the known resemblance and the inferred one there is some connection by means of causation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before accepting an analogical argument, demonstrate the causal connection that justifies transferring the inference. Examples of bad analogies include Pythagorean numerological inferences and attributing enlargement of a metropolis to disease because it resembles a heart; good metaphors may suggest proofs but cannot substitute for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor is not proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A metaphor is not to be considered as an argument, but as an assertion that an argument exists; it aids apprehension but does not itself prove the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors to clarify or suggest lines of proof, but do not treat vivid illustration as substitute for demonstration. Beware metaphors that rest on mere name-similarity (e.g., Bacon's river/valuation analogy) where parity of cause is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization — bad classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The most fertile source of fallacies of generalization is bad classification: bringing together in one group, under one name, things which have no common properties or none but such as are too unimportant to allow general propositions of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the predicate used to form a class is a stable, relevant property. Beware extending a familiar term by slight links to dissimilar cases (Bacon's Humidum example, the Greek κίνησις used to denote heterogeneous phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Ratiocination (deductive/syllogistic errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors seated in the ratiocinative or deductive part of inquiry — the rules of the syllogism are a complete protection against the more obvious forms of these fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate arguments into syllogistic form to expose illicit processes: watch for undistributed middle terms, illicit processes of the extremes, having more than three terms (hidden or explicit), and other vicious syllogistic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous conversion of propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple conversion errors such as inferring 'All B are A' from 'All A are B', or treating the converse of a hypothetical as valid (i.e., from 'If A then B' inferring 'If B then A').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept the converse of universals or hypotheticals without justification. Recognize that true conclusions do not prove the premises; apparent correctness of consequences can mislead into false acceptance of a doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing the premises (à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies introduced by slipping between syllogisms by changing or losing the qualifications/conditions of a premise: a proposition asserted with a qualification in the premises is used absolutely in the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When chaining arguments, track qualifications and necessary conditions (including temporal conditions). Examples: Mercantile theory misuses 'money brings riches' without its provisos; tithe/rent arguments drop conditional context; many misapplications of abstract truths arise this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misapplication of principles 'true in the abstract'
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a principle that is true only when 'all modifying causes are supposed absent' as if true absolutely, ignoring real-world modifying circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and make explicit background assumptions of abstract principles before applying them; treat them as conditional rules unless you can verify the absence of modifying causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of Ambiguity (equivocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Error arising when something true under one sense of a word is reasoned on as if true under another sense — ambiguity of terms causes reasoning to address different points under the illusion of unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully disambiguate key terms in an argument. Common problematic cases include paronymous words, etymological uses vs customary uses, and words with multiple technical vs popular senses. Test whether premises and conclusion use terms in the same sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous middle / Fallacia Figuræ Dictionis
rubrics_metrics.description: The fallacy built on paronymous or conjugate words — taking for granted that related forms (substantive, adjective, verb) have precisely corresponding meanings, leading to an invalid middle term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for shifts among related words that change meaning (e.g., 'project' vs 'projector', 'presume' vs 'presumption'); force explicit definitions of middle terms when mapping informal language into formal argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy from etymology
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a term in its etymological or original sense to dictate its present meaning in an argument (assuming the 'right meaning' must conform to the root verb's sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect customary/legal/technical meanings and usages rather than assuming archaic or literal derivations determine sense (example: 'representative').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish contrary vs contradictory propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusing the contrary of a proposition (two propositions that cannot both be true but may both be false) with its contradictory leads to the error of mistaking the reverse of wrong for right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train to state propositions explicitly to reveal whether opposition is contrary or contradictory; this exposes many practical mistakes in moral and political reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity in practical/technical vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical or practical phrases with multiple domain-specific senses (e.g., 'scarcity of money' meaning currency vs capital seeking investment) can create pseudo-problems and misdirect policy conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering contested policy claims or controversies, resolve the specific technical senses of terms before inferring policy implications (examples: 'scarcity of money', 'influence of property', 'theory', 'the Church').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use syllogistic form as a diagnostic tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Rendering an argument in syllogistic form helps ensure that suppressed premises and hidden assumptions are revealed, enabling the detection of fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an argument cannot be expressed without introducing an obviously false or unjustified premise, the arguer has been compelled to make a choice; use this to test the robustness of the position and to expose covert assumptions.
